hope.label: Hope and optimism
hope.insight: In the Prophetic way, hope is action, not waiting: the Prophet ﷺ loved good omens, and commanded planting the seedling even as the Hour is established. The Quran builds hope on the vastness of Allah's mercy: “My mercy encompasses all things,” and promises that hardship never comes alone: “Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease.”

now: Write down one small, specific goal to start on today
week: Tie the goal to a simple daily habit
Ask Allah for what you want with certainty
long: Hold on to “the deeds done most consistently, even if few”

questions: What is the smallest first step I can take right now?
avoid: Waiting for perfect conditions before starting

sin.label: Sin and repentance
sin.insight: In Islam the door of repentance does not close until the sun rises from the west, and Allah “stretches out His hand at night so that the one who sinned by day may repent.” Indeed, Allah rejoices at His servant's repentance more than a man who finds his lost camel in the desert. The most hopeful verse: “Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah.” Sincere repentance means regret, stopping and resolve, returning people's rights, “following a bad deed with a good one to wipe it out,” and changing one's environment, as in the story of the man who killed a hundred.

now: Make wudu, pray two units of prayer, and seek forgiveness with the master supplication for forgiveness
Follow the sin with an immediate good deed: charity, remembrance, kindness
Stay under the cover Allah has given you and do not expose yourself before people
week: Identify the gateways to the sin (place, time, person, app) and close one of them
If the sin involves someone's right, return it or ask their pardon wisely
Look for company that helps you
long: Build alternative habits that fill the space the sin used to fill
If you fall again, repent again: “the best of those who sin are those who repent”

questions: What usually comes before the sin: emptiness? Loneliness? Pressure?
Is my despair of repentance more dangerous to me than the sin itself?
avoid: Despairing of Allah's mercy after repeating the sin
Sinning openly or boasting about it
Delaying repentance until you “are ready”

waswasa.label: Intrusive thoughts and doubts
waswasa.insight: Intrusive whisperings do not mean weak faith. Indeed, the Prophet ﷺ told those who were horrified by their thoughts: “That is clear faith,” because your hatred of them is a sign of faith. And “Allah has pardoned my Ummah for what occurs to their minds, as long as they do not act upon it or speak of it.” The Prophetic remedy is to seek refuge with Allah and then “stop” — that is, to stop following the thought and not argue with it. The religion is ease, and being excessively hard on oneself in purification and prayer goes against the Sunnah.

now: Say: “I believe in Allah; I seek refuge with Allah from Satan, the outcast,” then turn immediately to another task
Do not debate the thought or try to prove its opposite
week: In purification and prayer, keep to the correct minimum and do not repeat because of doubt
Recite the last two surahs of the Quran morning and evening
long: If the whisperings consume hours of your day, OCD is a medical condition with effective treatment
Ask a trusted scholar about the concessions for someone with whisperings (doubt after finishing an act of worship is ignored)

questions: Do I hate these thoughts? (If yes, that is clear faith)
How much of my time goes on repeating things?
avoid: Arguing with the whisperings and trying to convince them
Giving in to the urge to repeat
Believing you are sinful because of thoughts you hate
waswasa.help: OCD is a common medical condition treated with behavioural therapy and sometimes medication; seeing a specialist does not contradict faith.

faith_weak.label: Weak faith and spiritual dryness
faith_weak.insight: The ups and downs of faith are human nature: Hanzalah said “Hanzalah has become a hypocrite,” and the Prophet ﷺ answered: “There is a time for this and a time for that.” The Prophet ﷺ himself would often say: “O Turner of the hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion.” The remedy in the Prophetic way: “the deeds most beloved to Allah are those done most consistently, even if few,” righteous company (“a man follows the religion of his close friend”), and praying for steadfastness.

now: Pray the next prayer on time, even without full focus; keeping it up comes first
Pray: “O Turner of the hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion”
week: Choose a very small act of worship and keep to it daily (one page of Quran, the morning remembrances)
Sit with someone who reminds you of Allah
long: Increase your worship gradually, without leaps that lead to dropping off
Learn the meanings of what you recite in prayer so your heart is present

questions: When was my faith at its best? What was different then?
What is the minimum I will never give up, however low I feel?
avoid: Abandoning worship altogether because you lack focus
Comparing yourself with the most devout people until you despair

burnout.label: Exhaustion and burnout
burnout.insight: Islam recognises the limits of human energy: “Allah does not charge a soul except with that within its capacity,” and affirms that your soul has a right over you, just as Allah and your family do (“so give each one who has a right their due”). The Prophet ﷺ disapproved of those who wanted to exhaust themselves even in worship — so how much more in other things? Prayer is rest, not a burden: “Give us rest through it, O Bilal,” and glorifying Allah before sleep was his advice ﷺ to his exhausted daughter.

now: Stop: take a real break away from screens, even for half an hour
Go to bed early tonight; sleep is your soul's right
Before sleeping, say Subhan Allah 33 times, Al-hamdu lillah 33 times and Allahu akbar 34 times
week: Write down all your responsibilities and drop, delegate or postpone three of them
Ask your family or colleagues for help, clearly
Set a limit on your working hours
long: Restore the balance between Allah's right, your own, your family's and your work's
Build a fixed weekly habit of rest

questions: What can I say “no” to this week?
Am I exhausting myself because it is truly necessary, or to please others or out of perfectionism?
avoid: Treating rest as laziness
Constantly sacrificing sleep and health
Refusing help out of pride

people_pleasing.label: Pleasing people and what they say
people_pleasing.insight: One of the most liberating principles for the heart: “Whoever seeks Allah's pleasure at the cost of people's displeasure, Allah will suffice him against the people.” Pleasing everyone is an unreachable goal, and the Prophet ﷺ taught Ibn ‘Abbas that if the whole nation gathered to benefit him or harm him, it could do only what Allah had written. Working for Allah's sake protects you from being crushed when you are not thanked: “We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We wish not from you reward or gratitude.”

now: The next time you are asked for something you do not want to do, say “I'll think about it” instead of an immediate “yes”
Remind yourself: Allah's pleasure is the measure
week: Practise saying “no” kindly in a small situation
Correct your intention in something you do in order to be praised
long: Build your self-worth on your relationship with Allah, not on people's opinions

questions: If no one knew what I was doing, would I still do it?
What do I really lose if this person gets upset with me?
avoid: Sacrificing your principles to please people
Confusing politeness with submission

marriage.label: Marital conflict
marriage.insight: In the Quran marriage is “tranquillity, affection and mercy,” and spouses are “clothing” for each other. The Prophetic way in marital conflict rests on: a balanced view (“A believing man should not hate a believing woman; if he dislikes one of her traits, he will be pleased with another”), attention to feelings (“I know when you are pleased with me and when you are angry with me”), forbearance in front of others (“Your mother became jealous”), sharing the housework (he served his family), then wise mediation when there is a rift (“send an arbitrator from his people and an arbitrator from her people”) — and “reconciliation is best.” And “the best of you is the best to his family.”

now: Postpone the discussion if either of you is angry: “When one of you is angry, let him be silent”
Write down: what exactly is bothering me? What do I need?
Name to yourself three good qualities in your spouse (“he will be pleased with another trait”)
week: Choose a calm moment and speak in the form “I feel…” rather than “You always…”
Take the first step with a small gesture of affection (a word, a gift, help at home)
Set aside time for just the two of you, without phones or children
long: If the conflict keeps returning without resolution, seek a wise arbitrator from the family or a marriage counsellor
Renew your affection through shared activities, as the Prophet ﷺ raced ‘A'ishah
Learn together the skills of dialogue and resolving disagreements

questions: Is the disagreement about the issue itself, or about the way we talk to each other?
What does my spouse need from me but does not say openly?
Am I trying to win the argument, or to protect the relationship?
avoid: Bringing family or friends into every disagreement
Threatening divorce or separation in a moment of anger
Arguing in front of the children
Comparing your spouse with other people's spouses
marriage.help: If there is repeated physical or emotional abuse, safety comes first: contact a protection service, or a family or legal professional.

jealousy_spouse.label: Jealousy and suspicion between spouses
jealousy_spouse.insight: Moderate jealousy comes from love; the Mothers of the Believers felt jealous, and the Prophet ﷺ dealt with it with forbearance and understanding. But the Quran warns against the chain of “suspicion, then spying”: “Avoid much assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy,” and commands verifying before judging: “investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.”

now: Do not confront on the basis of suspicion; write down what you know for certain and what you only suspect
Avoid going through the phone; it destroys trust more than it builds it
week: Express your feelings calmly: “I feel anxious when…” rather than “You are cheating on me”
Agree on clear boundaries that protect trust (privacy, contact with others)
long: If the jealousy is obsessive and repeated without evidence, consult a professional
Build trust through openness and mutual faithfulness

questions: Do I have real evidence, or are these inner fears?
Is my jealousy linked to past experiences rather than to my current spouse?
avoid: Spying and searching
Accusing without proof
Responding to jealousy with mockery or neglect
